post.title: The rephrase prompt matters more than the generator's size
post.content:
A 1B-parameter generator wrote better synthetic pretraining data than its 27B sibling. Not a tie, a reversal: 15.31 macro-average against 14.76, on the same task, same source, same everything except the model doing the rephrasing. An April 2026 study spanning generators from 135M to 27B parameters found the curve saturates early, and the variable that actually moved the needle was the rephrasing prompt.

That is the inversion worth sitting with. The reflex in synthetic-data work is to reach for the biggest available teacher and assume quality scales with it. This systematic sweep says the teacher's size hits diminishing returns around the 1B mark for this job, while the format you ask it to produce keeps paying out. The math-style prompt scored 15.31, a 1.54-point lift over the 13.77 DCLM baseline. Table format hit 14.83, FAQ 14.45, tutorial 14.30. The choice between those formats out-swings the choice between a 1B and a 27B generator.

Why would prompt beat scale? Rephrasing is not a knowledge task. The source document already carries the facts. The generator's job is to re-present them in a shape the downstream model learns from efficiently, and a 1B model is entirely capable of restructuring text into a clean table or a worked example. The extra 26B parameters buy reasoning the rephrase does not need. You were paying for capability that the task does not consume.

The scaled-up artifact backs it. The team generated 486 billion tokens this way into a dataset they call FinePhrase. The table variant peaked at 17.18 macro-average, a 3.41-point lift over DCLM. And because the generator is small, throughput is the quiet headline: 33.1 million tokens per GPU-hour against roughly 1.1 million for a heavier rephrasing baseline. That is close to a 30x cost difference for data that scored higher. Small generator, right prompt, and you get more tokens and better tokens at once.

One caveat I will not let slide. The format that wins is task-coupled. Math format topped a benchmark suite weighted toward reasoning. I would not assume the table prompt is universally best. The transferable claim is narrower and more useful: the prompt is the dominant design variable, so prompt selection deserves the search budget you were about to spend on a bigger teacher. The study also found mix-in dataset choice compressed quality gaps from 4.67 points down to 1.78, which says the same thing from another angle. What you ask for matters more than how big the thing answering is.

Pick the format before you pick the generator. The format is where the points are.

## Sources

- [research] [Niklaus et al. 2026, "How Can We Synthesize High-Quality Pretraining Data?" (arXiv:2604.13977)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13977)
